after: ## The equatorial climate and why it happens
alt: Side view from one Tropic to the other. At the Equator heated air rises in a low-pressure belt where the trade winds converge, cools and forms cumulonimbus cloud and heavy rain. Near the Tropics the air sinks in high-pressure belts, warms and holds its moisture, so skies stay clear over the hot deserts.
caption: Rising air at the Equator brings daily rain; the same air sinks near the Tropics and keeps deserts dry.

after: ## The equatorial climate and why it happens
alt: Four panels of one equatorial day. Clear morning sky; the high Sun heats the ground; warm air rises, cools and condenses into towering clouds; heavy afternoon thunderstorms fall from cumulonimbus clouds.
caption: Heating, rising, cooling, condensing: convection gives rain almost every afternoon.

after: ## The hot desert climate and why it happens
alt: West to east cross-section from the Pacific to the Andes. Sinking air under high pressure warms over the desert; a cold current offshore cools the air so it gives fog, not rain; moist air from the east rises and rains on the far side of the Andes, so the Atacama lies in a rain shadow. Below, five factors: sinking air, dry trade winds, distance from the sea, cold currents and rain shadow.
caption: Several factors usually combine to make a hot desert; the Atacama has three at once.

after: ## Worked example: describing a climatic graph
alt: Four numbered steps for describing a climatic graph, each with wording from the equatorial example: an overall statement, the maximum and minimum with months, the range or total, and the seasonal pattern. A final box shows how to explain: high Sun angle for high temperatures, low pressure and convection for rain every month.
caption: Overall picture, extremes with months, range or total, then the seasonal pattern.

alt: Cross-section of a rainforest with four layers: emergent trees up to about 50 m, a dense continuous canopy, an understorey of young trees and shrubs, and a dark forest floor. Buttress roots, a liana and an epiphyte are labelled. Below, four adaptations: drip tips, buttress roots, lianas and epiphytes, and thin smooth bark.
caption: Four layers, each with plants adapted to how much light reaches it.

alt: Two nutrient-cycle diagrams. In intact forest the biomass store is large and litter and soil stores are small; leaves fall, decay within weeks and are taken back up by shallow roots, while some nutrients are leached. After clearance the biomass store is gone and heavy rain erodes and leaches the soil, which becomes infertile within a few years.
caption: The nutrients live in the trees, so removing the trees removes the fertility.

alt: A desert succulent with a water-storing stem, spines or small waxy leaves, wide shallow roots near the surface and a long tap root down to groundwater. Beside it, the ephemeral cycle: seeds lie in the soil, rain falls, they germinate and flower, and set seed within weeks. A strip notes animals that are nocturnal or burrow, the fennec fox and the camel.
caption: Desert plants either reach water, catch it fast, store it or wait for it.

alt: Six causes of Amazon deforestation (cattle ranching, soya farming, logging, mining, roads and hydroelectric dams) lead to clearance of the canopy. Effects follow: soil is exposed, eroded and leached and becomes infertile within a few years; rivers silt and flood risk rises; habitats are lost; less transpiration can reduce rainfall; carbon dioxide is released; indigenous peoples lose land; but jobs, export income and roads are gained.
caption: Give effects as a chain, and weigh the costs against the gains.
